e.t: “Abiesdri” or “Aviezthri” is a personal name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs four times in the LXX corpus: once in Judges and three times in Daniel. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, its particular identity and role must be determined from the passage where it appears.

gl: that will not stand up to examination; unconsidered
d: that will not stand up to examination; unconsidered

e.t: This Greek LXX adjective describes something “that will not stand up to examination; unconsidered”—something accepted or treated without careful testing or thoughtful consideration. It characterizes a person, judgment, or claim as lacking examination rather than proving that the matter itself is false. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 21:18; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what it modifies there.

The word is the proper name “Ailim,” also rendered “Elim.” It identifies a named place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. As a proper name, its meaning is mainly its designation, not a broader concept to translate. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs seven times across five verses, appearing in Exodus, Numbers, and Isaiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “without labour; untiringly.” It describes how an action is carried out, emphasizing that it happens without tiring effort or laborious work. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 16:20. Its exact force depends on the action and sentence surrounding it, but its central idea remains that something is done freely and without weariness. It functions as a description of the manner in which an action occurs.

This Greek LXX noun means “locust” or “grasshopper,” referring to the familiar insect. It is used for an individual insect or for locusts considered as a group. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 32 times, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Judges, the Psalms, Jeremiah, Joel, and 2 Chronicles. Its normal meaning remains straightforward: a locust or grasshopper, without requiring a symbolic meaning apart from the surrounding passage.

This verb means “boil up”: it describes something rising, swelling, or becoming intensely active like liquid brought to a boil. Its central idea is upward, forceful movement rather than quiet existence. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, including three Old Testament passages and one deuterocanonical passage. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is described as boiling up, but the basic sense remains a vigorous rising or swelling.

This adjective means “for a man,” describing something associated with, intended for, or appropriate to a man. It appears 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this LXX corpus, so its basic sense is established across more than one book rather than being limited to a single passage. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a male-related or man-directed description.

This word means “without strength,” describing someone or something lacking the power or ability to act. It functions as a verb in the Greek Old Testament wording and is found once in the Greek Septuagint, at Isaiah 40:30. Its basic sense is weakness or inability rather than a particular kind of weakness; the surrounding verse is needed to determine how that condition is being applied there.

This noun means “helper” or “protector”—one who comes to another’s aid and provides safeguarding. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 18 times, chiefly in the Psalms, where its central idea remains assistance and defense. The word can describe someone relied upon for support rather than merely a casual assistant. Its use across these passages presents help as active and dependable, especially when protection or rescue is needed.

gl: slaughter by cutting off the head
d: slaughter by cutting off the head

e.t: This verb means “slaughter by cutting off the head.” It describes a violent act of killing, making the manner of death explicit rather than referring to killing in general. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 15:20. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning is clear: to kill by severing the head.

This verb means “launder off”: to wash something so that dirt or another unwanted substance is removed. It describes an action of cleansing rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in passages from Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being washed and the surrounding words, but its central idea remains the removal of what clings through washing.

This verb means “wear out”: to use something until it becomes worn, weakened, or exhausted. It describes an action rather than a person or object by itself, so the surrounding sentence identifies what is being worn out. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Hosea and once in Micah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains bringing something to a worn or depleted condition.

The adjective means “without stumbling”: it describes someone or something that moves without falling or losing footing. In ordinary language, it presents the absence of a stumble rather than an action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:39. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “make childless”: it describes causing someone to be without children. It functions as an action word, focusing on the effect produced in a person or family rather than simply describing a childless condition. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 18 verses, so it expresses a recognizable scriptural idea while remaining tied to particular contexts. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Achlai is a proper name, also given as Akhle. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:31. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name alone does not establish additional meaning about the person who bears it. Its normal function is simply to identify that individual within the biblical genealogy.

Balasan, also rendered Valasan, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 2:2. The available record does not provide the surrounding verse text, so it does not establish further details about this individual or the significance of the name. Its normal function is simply personal identification within the passage.

Bameth, also rendered Vameth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the LXX, at Joshua 19:8. Because it functions as a place-name, its meaning is primarily the location or name it designates, not an abstract concept that can be translated into an ordinary description.

Banounai, also rendered Vanune, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament and does not itself provide a broader definition or doctrinal meaning. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 10:14. Without the verse text or additional contextual information, the name alone does not reveal the person’s family, position, character, or role in that passage.

This word is a proper name referring to “Geththem,” also given as “Gethem.” It does not describe an action, quality, or relationship; it identifies a particular name in the Greek Old Testament text. The form remains unchanged rather than taking different grammatical endings. It occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Samuel 14:33. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its role there.

This Greek LXX proper noun is a name given as “Gerrēnoi; Yerrini.” It does not function as a general description like an action or quality word, but as a specific designation. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 13:24. Since the verse text and surrounding context are unavailable here, no more specific contextual sense can be stated responsibly. The spelling points to a named entity rather than an ordinary vocabulary term.

This noun means “training,” referring to deliberate exercise or discipline that develops strength and readiness. It describes purposeful preparation rather than casual activity. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 11:20. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains directed training or disciplined practice. It is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Greek New Testament entity.

This Greek LXX noun means “thicket” or “copse,” referring to a dense group of shrubs or trees. It names a kind of wooded growth rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel and Isaiah. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a small, dense woodland or brushy area.

Deblathaim is a proper name, rendered as “Deblathaim” or “Thevlathem.” It identifies a named place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs three times: twice in Numbers 33 and once in Jeremiah 31. The available wording preserves the name but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning for it.

This verb means “divide”: to separate something into distinct portions or groups. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly for the act of dividing, whether the object is people, possessions, land, or something being separated into parts. The word occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, from Genesis through 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being divided.

διασκευάζω means “get quite ready” or “equip”: it describes an action that makes someone or something prepared. As a verb, it expresses doing the preparing, not simply being ready. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, in Joshua and 1 Maccabees. The surrounding verse identifies what is being prepared, while the central idea remains thorough readiness or equipment.

This verb means “cleave”: it describes an act of cutting or separating something rather than naming a person, object, or quality. As a verb, it identifies an action performed on something. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Psalms and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb describes acting cunningly—using cleverness and craftiness rather than dealing openly. It refers to conduct marked by calculated skill, often suggesting that a person is not being straightforward. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times across four verses, appearing three times in Psalms and once in Numbers. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “spring,” the season of the year associated with the renewal and growth that follow winter. It is a noun naming that season, rather than an action or description. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, appearing in Genesis, Numbers, Psalms, Zechariah, and Wisdom. Its repeated rendering as “spring” confirms this consistent seasonal meaning across its uses. The precise force of the word in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “indict” and can express acting “without accusation.” It refers to bringing a charge against someone rather than merely describing a person or thing. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, across passages from Exodus, Proverbs, Zechariah, Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the person being accused.

This noun means “custom”: an established practice or accepted way of doing things. It can refer to a customary observance or pattern followed by a community or people. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in deuterocanonical books. The word’s basic sense remains focused on a practice shaped by repeated use, rather than on a single action or event. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This adverb means “pointlessly,” describing an action done without a useful purpose or worthwhile result. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs.35.25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains that the action lacks meaningful purpose.

This adjective means “hundred years old.” It describes a person or living thing by stating an age of one hundred years. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 17:17, so its basic meaning is especially clear and narrow rather than a broad description of many kinds of situations. The word functions as an age-description, identifying someone who has reached a century of life.

gl: change the constitution of a state; cause it to degenerate
d: change the constitution of a state; cause it to degenerate

e.h: Changing a State for the Worse
e.t: This verb means to change the constitution of a state, especially by causing it to degenerate. It describes an alteration in a community’s governing order, with the added sense that the change makes that order worse or less sound. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 4:19. The word therefore points to political or civic deterioration rather than an ordinary personal change; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding text.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “blow away.” It describes the action of moving something away by blowing, whether literally or as an image of something being driven off. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Ezekiel, Haggai, and Malachi, and also appears in Sirach and 4 Maccabees within the supplied Greek Scriptures. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains forceful removal by blowing.

This word means “less” or “inferior,” describing something that has a smaller amount, degree, size, or standing than another. As an adjective, it can describe a person or thing as lower in comparison; as an adverb, it can indicate a lesser extent or degree. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 24 times, often expressing comparison rather than an absolute absence or lack. Its precise force depends on what is being compared in the sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “ambush”: a hidden attack or concealed position from which someone waits to strike unexpectedly. It names the act or situation of lying in wait, rather than describing the person who carries it out. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, especially in Judges, where concealed attacks are repeatedly mentioned. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a planned attack carried out from concealment.

This Greek LXX verb means “related to.” It describes a connection or association between one thing and another, showing that something belongs with, concerns, or has a relation to something else. It functions as an action or state of being related, rather than as a name for a person or object. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Esther 8:1; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “six hundred,” expressing a numerical quantity. It is an adjective, so it describes or helps identify something counted as six hundred rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings of this corpus, it occurs 67 times, including passages that count people and other quantities. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding noun and sentence show exactly what is being counted.

This word means a promise: a stated assurance or commitment given by someone to another. As a noun, it names the promise itself rather than the act of promising. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, appearing in Esther, Psalms, Amos, 1 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “come to aid; defend.” It describes an active response to someone who needs help: a person does not merely feel concern but moves to assist or protect. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears twice, once in 3 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic force is the act of coming alongside another person in support or defense, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation.

This verb means “hang over”: something extends above, remains suspended over, or looms upon something below. It describes an action or condition rather than a person or object, so the surrounding sentence shows what is hanging over and what lies beneath it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Isaiah and once in Hosea. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains something positioned above and continuing over another thing.

This Greek LXX verb means to be “mad after” something or to “dote upon” it, describing an intense, excessive attachment or infatuation. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 7:5. Because no verse text is included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its surrounding passage, but its basic sense is passionate, captivated desire rather than neutral interest.

Esedek, also rendered Esethek, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it identifies a particular person or place by name. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 19:10. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name’s specific referent must be determined from that passage, but its basic function is clear: it serves as a named designation, not as a translatable common noun.

This Greek LXX adjective means “well-girdled.” It describes a person or group as properly or securely girded, emphasizing a condition of being equipped with a firmly fastened girdle. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Joshua and Sirach. Because the available meaning is brief and no verse text is provided, its precise significance in each passage depends on what is being described there. Its central idea remains someone or something made ready and secure by being well-girded.

This LXX word means “straight” or “directly.” As an adjective, it can describe something that is straight; as an adverb, it describes an action done directly or without turning aside. It occurs 63 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing especially in Psalms, Isaiah, and Proverbs. Its basic sense can describe a straight course or direct action, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described.

This word is the proper name “Ēlias,” or Elias, identifying a person rather than describing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: once in Malachi, twice in Sirach, and once in 1 Maccabees. The name itself supplies identification; the surrounding verse is needed to understand what is being said about Elias in each passage.

This noun means heat: the condition or quality of being hot. It names heat as a thing rather than describing an action, person, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 2:4. The word is rendered “heat,” matching its direct sense. This is its only occurrence in that corpus. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text.

Iachan, also rendered Iakhan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies one individual and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 5:13. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or spiritual concept; its meaning is simply the person designated by this name in the biblical record.

Idithoun is a proper name, rendered “Idithoun” or “Ithithun.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times: once in 2 Chronicles and three times in Psalms. Because the available material gives the name but not its meaning or the surrounding verse text, it is best understood simply as the personal name Idithoun or Ithithun. Its precise role in any particular passage depends on that passage’s context.

“Iebous” or “Ievus” is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). It identifies a named subject rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs six times in the LXX corpus, across Joshua, Judges, and 1 Chronicles. Because the word is a name and no verse text is provided here, its precise referent in each passage depends on the surrounding context.

Iektan is a proper name identifying a person named Iektan in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the individual it names. This name occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all within Genesis 10:25, 10:26, and 10:29. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain Iektan’s particular role in each passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Iodom” or “Iothom.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:23. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s role or significance in that passage. Its normal function is simply to designate the individual named Iodom or Iothom.

Isoua, also rendered Isua, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 7:30. Since the available record does not include the verse text or surrounding context, its specific family connection or role there cannot be explained from the name alone.

Issaar is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears 11 times across 11 verses, and its English rendering is consistently “Issaar” where a rendering is recorded. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and family or historical context, which is not included here. The word itself functions as a personal designation, not as a general vocabulary term.

This Greek LXX adjective means “weary” or “wearied,” describing someone exhausted, worn down, or lacking strength. It can describe a condition brought about by labor, hardship, or prolonged distress. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings: twice in Job and once in 2 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense remains focused on weariness rather than defining the particular cause, which must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to “that which is prepared”—something made ready or arranged for use. It names a prepared thing rather than describing the action of preparing it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 32:6. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be described further; its basic meaning remains a thing that has been prepared.

This adjective describes someone who is in affliction, distressed, or grieved. It points to an inward state of sorrow or suffering rather than an action performed by someone else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four different verses, and is rendered “grieved” in several of those occurrences. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a condition of deep distress or grief.

This Greek LXX noun means “tile,” referring to a piece used in building or covering a structure. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 2 Samuel 17:28. The word identifies a physical building material rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is straightforward: a tile used as part of a roof or structure.

This word means “dust,” referring to loose, dry particles. It is a noun used to name dust as a physical substance in the Greek Old Testament. The word appears ten times in ten Old Testament verses, showing a recurring but relatively limited vocabulary item rather than a broad range of meanings. Its central sense remains consistent wherever it occurs, while the surrounding verse determines how the dust is being mentioned. It first appears in Exodus 9:9 and last appears in Song of Songs 3:6.

This Greek LXX verb means “tell” or “declare”: to communicate words or make something known. It describes the act of speaking or reporting, whether a person is conveying information, announcing something, or expressing what is to be said. The word functions as a verb, so it presents telling or declaring as an action. It is widely used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, occurring 2,295 times in this LXX corpus. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being communicated and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “leprous” when describing a person or condition, and “leper” when referring to a person affected by it. It is an adjective that can function as a description of someone marked by leprosy. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, especially in Leviticus, where it is associated with identifying and dealing with a leprous person, and also in historical passages concerning individuals called lepers. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Lomna is a proper name, rendered as “Lomna.” The available lexical information identifies it as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs three times, appearing once each in 2 Kings 19:8, 2 Chronicles 21:10, and Isaiah 37:8. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its normal lexical function is simply to designate Lomna by name.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Magedōn” or “Mayethon.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general idea, action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Joshua and once in 2 Chronicles. The name’s precise referent and significance must be determined from the surrounding passage, since the available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a fuller definition.

This noun means “Second Quarter.” It refers to a specific designation rather than describing an action, quality, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 22:14. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its exact local significance cannot be explained further; however, the lexical meaning identifies the term as “Second Quarter,” a named or defined section associated with that reference.

This Greek LXX noun means “fight” or “battle”—a contest or conflict between opposing sides. It can refer to open physical combat, but its normal meaning is broad enough to describe strife or contention as well. The word occurs 31 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with uses distributed across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains conflict between opposing parties.

This noun means an intoxicating drink—beverage capable of producing drunkenness or intoxication. It refers to a kind of drink rather than to the act of drinking or to a person who is drunk. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages in Judges, 1 Samuel, Jeremiah, Hosea, and Micah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “reconsideration” or “yielding”—a change in one’s mind or position rather than stubbornly continuing in the same direction. As a noun, it names that response or disposition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times: once in Proverbs, three times in Wisdom, and once in Sirach. Its precise emphasis can depend on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is turning from a former position by reconsidering it or yielding.

This noun means “cud,” referring to the food an animal brings back up and chews again. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears eleven times, chiefly in the dietary instructions of Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Its use identifies a recognizable animal characteristic in those passages, helping distinguish animals described as chewing the cud from others. The word itself names this specific substance or process, rather than expressing a moral quality, action, or personal title.

This LXX verb means “young,” describing someone or something in terms of youth. As a verb, it expresses the condition or activity of being young rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:31. The available lexical meaning is clear, while the precise force of that single use depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Odorra, also known as Othorra, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament translation. It identifies a named subject rather than describing an action, quality, or general category. The name appears only once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Genesis 10:27. Since no verse text or wider context is provided here, its cached meaning is limited to identifying this name and its alternate form.

This Greek LXX word is an exclamatory cry: “oh!” It expresses a sudden spoken reaction, rather than naming a person, object, or action. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, including Esther, Jeremiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning is the brief exclamation “oh!”

This word means “fog,” the cloudlike haze that obscures what can otherwise be seen. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures for a visible atmospheric covering. The word occurs ten times in this LXX corpus, including passages from Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Joel, Amos, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains the same wherever it appears: a dense veil or vapor that limits clear sight. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is describing ordinary weather or imagery drawn from fog’s obscuring character.

Ouesbi or Uezvi is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament text. It does not describe a general quality or action but identifies a particular person or name-bearer in the biblical record. This form appears once in the Septuagint at 2 Samuel 17:27. Without the surrounding verse text and a broader name identification provided here, its meaning is the proper name itself.

This Greek LXX noun means “deposit”: something entrusted to another person or held in another’s care. It names the thing placed there, rather than the action of handing it over. In this LXX corpus, it occurs five times, in Exodus, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. The word’s precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This verb means “hew”: to cut or shape something by striking it with a tool. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Kings 6:1. The word’s basic sense is therefore a direct action of cutting or shaping material, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being hewn.

This word means to form, shape, or contrive something. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes bringing something into a made or arranged condition, whether referring to creation, the shaping of people or things, or an intentional design. It occurs 52 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures, with additional occurrences in the deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains purposeful forming rather than mere existence. [p03:word:lxx:L710503:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710503:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L710503:reference:0]

This verb means “besiege”: to surround a city or stronghold with an attacking force, cutting it off and pressing it toward surrender. It describes sustained military pressure rather than a brief assault. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 23 times, including accounts of armies surrounding fortified places. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the encirclement and attack of a defended place.

This Greek LXX verb means “add” or “continue.” It describes putting something more with what is already present, or carrying an action forward. Thus, it can refer either to increasing something or to doing something further. The word occurs 262 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that both uses belong to its normal range. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being added or continued in the surrounding sentence.

Raaia, also rendered Rhaea, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:50. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish further details about the person or communicate a broader concept. Its meaning here is therefore its function as an individual name.

This Greek LXX verb means “gore” or “burst,” describing something breaking open or bursting through with force. It can refer to a forceful rupture rather than a quiet opening. The word occurs 36 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is bursting or being broken open there.

Saemērōn is a proper name, preserved in English as “Saemērōn” or “Saemiron.” It identifies a particular named referent in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This form occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 16:24. The name’s precise referent and significance must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text; the word itself functions simply as a name.

Salōm is a proper name, rendered “Salom,” used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. It functions as a personal designation rather than as a general description, action, or quality. The name occurs 11 times across 10 verses in this Greek LXX corpus, appearing especially in 1 Chronicles, with additional occurrences in Jeremiah, Baruch, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding genealogy or narrative.

Segoub, also rendered Seguv, is a personal name identifying an individual rather than a general idea or action. The name is given as “Segoub; Seguv,” so its meaning is best understood as the person’s designation. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times: once in 1 Kings and twice in 1 Chronicles. The available verse context does not provide enough information here to describe the person’s role or significance beyond this name.

Selna is a proper name, referring to a person named Selna rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 6:42. Because the available record gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, it does not establish additional meaning beyond identifying Selna as a named individual. The name is rendered “Selna,” preserving it as a personal designation rather than translating it into another descriptive term.

This adjective means “dark,” describing the absence or reduction of light. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe something physically shadowed or obscure, while the surrounding passage determines the precise sense in a particular verse. It occurs 15 times across 15 Old Testament verses, including passages in Genesis, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Proverbs, and Daniel. The word’s basic idea remains darkness or a dark condition rather than a separate spiritual meaning by itself.

This word means “roof,” the covering that forms the top of a building or shelter. It is a noun naming a physical part of a house or other structure, rather than an action or abstract idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, across Genesis, Ezekiel, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the roof or upper covering of a structure.

e.t: This word means a person who had charge of the sacred vestments, or a keeper of the sacred robes. It is a noun naming someone entrusted with caring for garments set apart for worship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 10:22. Its central idea is responsibility for preserving and managing sacred clothing, rather than describing the clothing itself or a general clothing attendant.

This verb means “break” or “crush,” describing an action that damages or separates something through force. As a verb, it presents breaking or crushing as an action rather than as an object, person, or place. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah 27:23 and once in Ezekiel 29:7. These references show its use in two Old Testament passages, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular force or outcome in either passage.

This word means “wild swine; boar,” referring to a large, wild pig rather than a domesticated animal. It is a noun, so it names the creature itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 79:14. The approved English rendering there is “boar,” which confirms the ordinary animal sense. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: a wild pig or boar.

This word is a proper name identifying Sōēa, also rendered Sia. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal or identifying name in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once, in Ezra 2:44, so its meaning is chiefly its identity rather than a broader concept developed through repeated use. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain whether it names a person, family, or group.

This Greek LXX noun refers to courage—the boldness or resolve to undertake something difficult. It describes an inner readiness to act with confidence rather than shrink back. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, including two occurrences in Job and one in 2 Maccabees. Its central idea is daring initiative: a person possesses the courage needed to take on a challenging task or situation. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to treat someone with insolence—to insult or behave toward them in a disrespectful way. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it describes an action rather than a person or object. It occurs six times: four times in Old Testament verses and twice in Deuterocanonical verses. Its central idea is contempt expressed through conduct or words; the surrounding passage determines who is dishonored and how the insult is carried out.

This verb means to bear up under something—to endure or carry a burden without giving way. It describes the act of supporting or withstanding what is difficult. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 20 times, so its central idea is established across several passages rather than being limited to one setting. The precise object being endured depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself focuses on patiently bearing what has been placed upon someone.

Phaltias, also rendered Faltias, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel chapter 11. The name appears at Ezekiel 11:1 and 11:13. Its meaning is therefore its identification of a named individual; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role in each passage.

This adjective describes someone who loves his own life and can therefore be characterized as cowardly. It points to a self-protective concern for preserving one’s life, rather than courage in facing danger or loss. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only once, at Wisdom 11:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic meaning centers on strong attachment to life and the fearful conduct associated with it.

This Greek LXX noun means “planting”—the act or result of putting a plant into the ground. It names planting as a thing rather than describing someone’s action. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in 2 Kings, Ezekiel, and Micah. Its occurrences are connected with the language of cultivated plants and their placement, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding text.

This Greek LXX verb means “detect” or “discover”—to recognize or uncover something previously hidden, unnoticed, or unknown. It describes finding something out rather than merely possessing knowledge. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines what is detected or discovered in each use, but the central idea remains the uncovering or recognition of something.

This verb means “prophesy”: to speak or declare a prophetic message. It describes the act of prophesying rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 45:4. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the action of delivering a prophecy.
